Now let me compile all the research into a comprehensive verse-by-verse commentary. I have material from enduringword.com (Guzik/Pentecostal), preceptaustin.org (Evangelical), John Gill (Baptist), Matthew Henry (Reformed/Puritan), Pulpit Commentary (Anglican), and Dr. Constable (Evangelical/DTS).

---

# Judges 10 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

## vv. 1–2: Tola the Minor Judge

**v. 1 — "After the time of Abimelech, a man of Issachar, Tola son of Puah, the son of Dodo, rose up to save Israel. He lived in Shamir, in the hill country of Ephraim."**

- **The transition from Abimelech:** Tola "arose to save" Israel. The Pulpit Commentary notes that Tola was raised up "to defend" Israel, perhaps not from a great invasion but from frequent border wars requiring an able chief to maintain independence. The exact enemies are untold. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/judges/10.htm)
- **No external enemy named:** Precept Austin notes that after Abimelech's atrocious, abominable reign, Israel needed a "savior." The oppression was not so much from without but from within — there is no record of external oppression for the minor judges. Their function was more to handle administrative and judicial matters than to fight wars. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_10_commentary)
- **John Gill** observes that though no specific enemies are mentioned, Tola may have saved Israel by composing the differences and dissensions Abimelech caused and recovering them from idolatry. His name is the same as Issachar's eldest son, and his father Puah bore the name of Issachar's second son. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/10.htm)
- **The name "Tola":** The Hebrew *tola* means "worm" or "scarlet stuff." Precept Austin adds a Messianic connection: in Psalm 22:6 the Messiah cries, "I am a worm" (*tola*). The worm (*tola*) dies on a tree giving birth to its young, leaving a red stain — a striking picture of Christ on the cross. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_10_commentary)
- **Shamir in Ephraim:** Though Tola was of Issachar, he dwelt in Ephraim. Pulpit says this was to distinguish it from Shamir in Judah. Gill says he moved to be centrally located, near the tabernacle at Shiloh, so people from all tribes could come for justice. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/judges/10.htm; https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/10.htm)
- **Tola is the second of the "minor judges"** (along with Shamgar, Jair, Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon). Between Tola and Jair, 45 years of stable rule are recorded with little detail. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_10_commentary)

**v. 2 — "Tola judged Israel twenty-three years, and when he died, he was buried in Shamir."**

- **A quiet, faithful tenure:** Matthew Henry says, "Quiet and peaceable reigns, though the best to live in, yield least variety of matter to be spoken of. Such were the days of Tola and Jair. They were humble, active, and useful men, rulers appointed of God." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/judges/10.htm)
- **Ellicott** notes the recurrence of "he judged" (*shaphat*) shows Tola was an honourable judge (*Suffes*), not a despot like Abimelech. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/10-2.htm)
- **23 years:** Dr. Constable observes no mention of Yahweh "raising him up" appears (unlike earlier judges), yet this brief notation pictures him as a worthy individual who enjoyed an orderly and stable tenure. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-10.html)
- Precept Austin notes it is surprising that it does not say "the land was undisturbed," as with previous judges, nor that "when the judge died Israel did evil again" — those formulaic elements are missing. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_10_commentary)

---

## vv. 3–5: Jair the Gileadite

**v. 3 — "Tola was followed by Jair the Gileadite, who judged Israel twenty-two years."**

- **Jair the Gileadite:** Gill notes Jair was of the half-tribe of Manasseh on the east side of Jordan — the first judge from Transjordan. God showed that though Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh were separated by the river, they were not neglected. Judges were raised up where oppression was greatest; Gilead was vulnerable to Ammonites. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/10.htm)
- **His name:** Constable says it means "may [God] enlighten." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-10.html)
- **Not the same Jair as in Moses' day:** Gill argues against identifying him with the Jair of Numbers 32:41, who would have lived over 300 years earlier. Rather, this Jair was a descendant who inherited and expanded those cities. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/10.htm)

**v. 4 — "He had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys. And they had thirty towns in the land of Gilead, which to this day are called Havvoth-jair."**

- **Wealth and polygamy:** David Guzik observes that Jair was a polygamous man of wealth and prestige. His many sons had prestigious transportation (donkeys) and their own territory to rule. Jair never took the title of king, but acted like one. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-10/)
- **Riding on donkeys:** Constable notes this marked them as having distinguished rank — in times when Israel had no horses, only the wealthy and prominent rode donkeys. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-10.html)
- **Gill** adds that these sons may have been appointed as judges under their father, riding circuit to administer justice in the various parts of the country, much like Samuel's sons (1 Sam 8:1). (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/10.htm)
- **"Havvoth-jair":** Means "the villages of Jair." The Pulpit Commentary notes a Hebrew wordplay: the word for "ass colts" (*ayarim*) is identical in consonants to the word for "cities" (*arim*) as pointed, reflecting the same literary mind that produced Jotham's fable and Samson's riddle. Ellicott says these villages were already named from an earlier Jair, but the old name was "revived and confirmed" on this occasion. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/judges/10.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/10-3.htm)
- **Canaanite cultural influence:** Constable observes that Jair's lifestyle — polygamy, many sons ruling cities — reflects continuing tendencies toward the lifestyle of surrounding pagan nations and away from fidelity to Yahweh. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-10.html)

**v. 5 — "When Jair died, he was buried in Kamon."**

- **Kamon:** The Pulpit Commentary says Josephus identifies it as a city of Gilead, but its exact site is unverified. Polybius mentions a "Camoun" among Transjordanian places. The careful recording of burial places of judges and kings is notable, beginning with Gideon (Judg 8:32). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/judges/10.htm)

## v. 6: Israel's Seven-fold Apostasy

**v. 6 — "And again the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD. They served the Baals, the Ashtoreths, the gods of Aram, Sidon, and Moab, and the gods of the Ammonites and Philistines. Thus they forsook the LORD and did not serve Him."**

- **"Did evil again":** The Pulpit Commentary notes that Tola and Jair had used their influence to maintain Jehovah's worship, but at their death idolatry broke out with more virulence than ever — not only the Baals and Ashtoreths but new forms of idol-worship from every neighbouring nation. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/judges/10.htm)
- **Seven gods listed:** David Guzik notes seven different ethnic and national gods mentioned, showing Israel's seven-fold apostasy. The phrase "did evil in the sight of the LORD" is repeated seven times in Judges. Israel worshipped these gods because they promised wealth (Baal) and romance (Ashtoreth), and "because everyone else was doing it." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-10/)
- **Symmetry of seven oppressions, seven gods:** The Pulpit Commentary notes the seven kinds of idols correspond symmetrically with seven retributive oppressions listed in vv. 11–12. Ellicott likewise observes this symmetry. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/10-6.htm)
- **Names of the gods:** The Pulpit Commentary identifies them: the gods of Syria (Aram) included Rimmon (2 Kings 5:18); the gods of Sidon were Baal and Ashtoreth with different rites; Chemosh of Moab; Milcom/Molech of Ammon; Dagon of the Philistines. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/judges/10.htm)
- **"They forsook the LORD and did not serve Him":** Gill observes this was worse than before: at other times they served other gods *alongside* the Lord, but now they had wholly forsaken Him, making no pretence of worshipping Him. Guzik adds: "When a man stops believing in God, he does not believe in nothing; he believes in anything." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/10.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-10/)
- **A new low:** Constable notes this is the last and longest list of Israel's sins. The only contiguous neighbour not listed as a negative influence is Edom. This was syncretism that in many cases involved total abandonment of Yahweh worship. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-10.html)

---

## vv. 7–9: God Sells Israel to the Philistines and Ammonites

**v. 7 — "So the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and He sold them into the hands of the Philistines and Ammonites."**

- **Two oppressors at once:** Constable notes this is the first time God handed His people into the power of *two* nations simultaneously — Philistines from the west and Ammonites from the east. "The anger of the LORD was hot" appears for the first time since Judges 3:8, signaling the climax of Israel's Canaanization. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-10.html)
- **"He sold them":** Guzik says: if Israel wanted to serve the gods of the Philistines and Ammonites, God would allow them to do so — in the fullest sense — by selling them into servitude to those very peoples. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-10/)
- **Gill** explains "sold" means they became subject and in bondage as slaves are; those west of the land fell to the Philistines, those east to the Ammonites. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/10.htm)

**v. 8 — "who that very year harassed and oppressed the Israelites, and did so for eighteen years to all the Israelites on the other side of the Jordan in Gilead, the land of the Amorites."**

- **Eighteen years of oppression:** Gill says these eighteen years of oppression are not to be reckoned into Jair's years, but from his death to the raising up of Jephthah. The Ammonites oppressed the Transjordan tribes — Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/10.htm)
- Constable dates this oppression at approximately 1123–1105 B.C. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-10.html)

**v. 9 — "The Ammonites also crossed the Jordan to fight against Judah, Benjamin, and the house of Ephraim, and Israel was in deep distress."**

- **Expansion of oppression:** Gill notes the Ammonites were not content with oppressing the Transjordan tribes but crossed the Jordan to ravage Canaan proper, targeting the tribes closest to the crossing — Judah, Benjamin, and Ephraim. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/10.htm)
- Matthew Henry sees this as the fulfillment of the warning in Leviticus 26:17, 37 — that Israel would have no power to stand before their enemies. "By their evil ways and their evil doings they procured this to themselves." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/judges/10.htm)

---

## vv. 10–14: Israel's Cry and God's Refusal

**v. 10 — "Then the Israelites cried out to the LORD, saying, 'We have sinned against You, for we have indeed forsaken our God and served the Baals.'"**

- **Incomplete repentance:** Guzik observes that the words of this cry seem fine, but God's response shows He saw something lacking. "One may cry out to the LORD, yet really just wish things were different. Crying out to God with the voice is not necessarily the same as crying out to Him with the heart." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-10/)
- **For the first time, Israel explicitly confesses sin.** Constable notes they had waited 18 years before appealing for help — compared to only 7 years against Midian (Judg 6:6) — indicating their hearts had become even harder. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-10.html)
- **Gill** says the distress opened their eyes to a sense of their sins as the cause, bringing confession of both omission (forsaking God) and commission (serving Baals). (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/10.htm)

**v. 11 — "The LORD replied, 'When the Egyptians, Amorites, Ammonites, Philistines,'"**

- **God's past deliverances:** God lists seven groups He delivered them from, corresponding to the seven false gods in v. 6. Gill notes Jarchi made this observation: seven salvations in opposition to seven idolatries. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/10.htm)
- **The communication:** Gill suggests the Lord spoke either by a prophet (cf. Judg 6:8), an angel, or even a theophany — "the uncreated one, the Son and Word of God, who might appear in human form." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/10.htm)

**v. 12 — "'Sidonians, Amalekites, and Maonites oppressed you and you cried out to Me, did I not save you from their hands?'"**

- **Maonites:** Gill identifies these either as the old inhabitants of Maon in the mountains of Judah, or more likely the Minaeans, an Arabian people mentioned by Strabo and Diodorus Siculus, perhaps allied with the Midianites. The Pulpit Commentary does not identify them definitively. Constable says the Septuagint renders them as "Midianites" (chs. 6–8). (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/10.htm; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-10.html)

**v. 13 — "'But you have forsaken Me and served other gods, so I will no longer save you.'"**

- **A conditional threat:** Gill clarifies "I will deliver you no more" is not absolute but conditional — "unless they repented of their idolatries, and forsook them." Constable likewise says this must be understood conditionally, as with all divine threatenings that imply "a reserve of mercy to the truly repentant" (cf. Jer 18:5–12; Jonah 3:4). (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/10.htm; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-10.html)
- **Tough love:** Guzik says God was harsh "because they had to be genuinely sick of their sin before they would genuinely turn to God." He quotes G. Campbell Morgan: "For the first time it is recorded that He refused to save them… In the message of His anger there was clearly evident a purpose of love." And Cundall: "This apparent rejection… was designed to test the sincerity of their response." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-10/)
- Matthew Henry: "God is able to multiply men's punishments according to the numbers of their sins and idols." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/judges/10.htm)

**v. 14 — "'Go and cry out to the gods you have chosen. Let them save you in your time of trouble.'"**

- **Ironic command:** Gill says God is not serious but speaks "in an ironical or sarcastic way" — calling on them to seek help from gods in whose power it was not to relieve them. Matthew Poole (quoted by Guzik) adds: "You have not been forced to worship these gods by your oppressors and tyrants; but you have freely chosen these gods before me." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/10.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-10/)

---

## vv. 15–16: True Repentance and God's Mercy

**v. 15 — "'We have sinned,' the Israelites said to the LORD. 'Deal with us as You see fit; but please deliver us today!'"**

- **Genuine surrender:** Guzik says this indicates total surrender: "The prayer that comes most naturally to us is, 'Do to me whatever seems best to me.'" They now submit to whatever God deems right, trusting His character. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-10/)
- Matthew Henry: "They acknowledged what they deserved, yet prayed to God not to deal with them according to their deserts. We must submit to God's justice, with a hope in his mercy." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/judges/10.htm)
- Gill observes they chose to fall into the hands of God rather than men, ready to accept famine or pestilence if God so willed, but pleading to be delivered from human enemies. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/10.htm)

**v. 16 — "So they put away the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD, and He could no longer bear the misery of Israel."**

- **"Fruits meet for repentance":** The Pulpit Commentary says this was the intended result of the severe but loving correction — putting away the foreign gods (cf. Gen 35:2; 1 Sam 7:3). Matthew Henry: "True repentance is not only for sin, but from sin." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/judges/10.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/judges/10.htm)
- **"His soul was grieved":** The Pulpit Commentary explains the Hebrew phrase literally means "was shortened" — He could bear it no longer. It occurs also in Numbers 21:4; Judges 16:16; Zechariah 11:2. A similar description of divine relenting appears in Hosea 11:7–9. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/judges/10.htm)
- **God's compassion:** Guzik says: "God looked upon disobedient Israel with compassion, not hatred. It was 'difficult' for God to allow Israel to stay in their misery, though it was best for them. Like the perfect loving parent, God hated to see Israel suffer, even when suffering was good for them." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-10/)
- Gill adds that this is anthropopathic language: grief properly does not belong to God (who has no passions), but it describes God acting in ways that resemble human sympathy — a change in the dispensations of His providence according to His unchangeable will. Maimonides understood it as the good will and pleasure of God to cease afflicting them. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/10.htm)
- **Precept Austin** highlights this remarkable statement: "His soul could no longer endure the misery of Israel" — Almighty God was Himself in pain over His people's suffering. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_10_commentary)

---

## vv. 17–18: The Gathering for Battle and the Search for a Leader

**v. 17 — "Then the Ammonites were called to arms and camped in Gilead, and the Israelites assembled and camped at Mizpah."**

- **A new chapter begins:** The Pulpit Commentary says this verse ought to begin a new chapter — the preliminary matter is concluded, and the history of deliverance by Jephthah begins. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/judges/10.htm)
- **Mizpah:** The Pulpit Commentary identifies Mizpah of Gilead as the same place where Laban and Jacob parted (Gen 31:25, 49), also called Ramoth-Mizpeh (Josh 13:26), Ramoth in Gilead (Josh 20:8), and later Ramoth-Gilead (1 Kings 4:13; 22:3). The name means "watch-tower," situated on a height in the tribe of Gad. It was the place of national meeting for all Gilead. The modern site is thought to be es-Salt, though not confirmed. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/judges/10.htm)
- A new spirit was aroused among the Israelites. By whatever channel God's reproach came (vv. 11–14), an answer of peace had also come upon their repentance, and they were emboldened to resist. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/judges/10.htm)

**v. 18 — "And the rulers of Gilead said to one another, 'Whoever will launch the attack against the Ammonites will be the head of all who live in Gilead.'"**

- **A leaderless army:** Guzik observes: "Israel gathered but had no leader. God's pattern for doing great works among His people is to raise up a man. He could do the work all by Himself; He could send angels… Yet God's normal means of operating is to raise up a man, and through that man to do a great work. God uses leaders." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-10/)
- **"The people and princes":** The Pulpit Commentary notes there is no "and" in the Hebrew. It should read "the assembly of the chiefs of Gilead" — the first step was to find a competent leader and agree to appoint him as permanent head and captain. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/judges/10.htm)
- **A carnal approach:** Constable adds a critical note: "Even though the Israelites had confessed their sin and repented genuinely, they approached this battle carnally. Rather than inquiring of God for strategy, the Israelites looked among themselves for a human leader whom they could persuade to lead them, by promising him kingship as a reward (cf. Judg 1:1). They were rejecting Yahweh's authority over them by doing this (cf. 1 Sam 8:7)." They would soon learn the man they chose had glaring weaknesses. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-10.html)
- Gill says this proclamation was made to encourage some person to take command and go before them to battle, promising him the governorship over all the tribes on that side of Jordan. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/10.htm)

## Distinctive Readings Across Traditions

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word — David Guzik)
- Emphasises God's "tough love" and the emotional dynamic between God and His people. God's refusal to deliver is a "shock tactic" to produce genuine repentance.
- The emphasis on God's pattern of raising up *a man* as leader (v. 18): "God uses leaders."
- Sees a personal, relatable God whose "soul could no longer endure the misery of Israel." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-10/)

### Reformed / Baptist (John Gill, Matthew Henry)
- **Gill** (Reformed Baptist): Emphasises divine sovereignty — God "sold" them, and His threatenings are conditional. He stresses that references to God's "grief" or "anger" are anthropopathic; God has no passions. "I will deliver you no more" is not absolute but conditional on repentance. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/10.htm)
- **Matthew Henry** (broadly Reformed/Puritan): Stresses that quiet, peaceable reigns like Tola's and Jair's are the best to live in, even if they yield little "variety of matter." He emphasises true repentance as being "not only for sin, but from sin." He sees the oppression as direct fulfillment of the covenant curses in Leviticus 26. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/judges/10.htm)

### Anglican (Pulpit Commentary)
- Attends carefully to textual detail: the Hebrew wordplay between "ass colts" and "cities," the lack of "and" in v. 18, the identification of Mizpah with Ramoth-Gilead.
- Emphasises the careful recording of burial sites as a notable feature of the narrative.
- Sees a literary symmetry: seven gods (v. 6) matched by seven deliverances (vv. 11–12). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/judges/10.htm)

### Evangelical / Dispensational (Dr. Constable)
- Views the minor judges as teaching two lessons: negatively, they maintained the status quo and did not reverse Israel's decline; positively, they show God's gracious blessing of apostate people in spite of themselves.
- Notes the literary structure: the formulaic expressions of the Judges cycle break down as the narrative progresses, reflecting the moral disintegration of Israel.
- Critical of Israel in v. 18: promising kingship as a reward for a military champion was effectively "rejecting Yahweh's authority." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-10.html)
